title: Measuring Your Net Promoter Score
supports: Opened with WebFetch. The likelihood-to-recommend question on a 0 to 10 scale; promoters 9 to 10, passives 7 to 8, detractors 0 to 6; NPS is the percentage of promoters minus the percentage of detractors; can be tracked by product, store, segment, region or team; trademarks held by Bain & Company, NICE Systems and Fred Reichheld. Vendor page; growth claims on it are not used.

title: Three Types of Net Promoter Scores
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Competitive benchmark NPS (double-blind, third party), relationship NPS (no trigger, once or twice a year) and experience NPS (triggered by an action, for immediate service recovery); survey a customer no more than once every three months; relationship and experience scores feed closed-loop follow-up; do not compare relationship and experience scores directly.

title: The One Number You Need to Grow (Frederick F. Reichheld, Harvard Business Review, December 2003)
supports: Opened with WebFetch (paywalled; summary and opening only). Author Fred Reichheld of Bain & Company; December 2003; argues companies spend heavily on complex satisfaction measures while measuring the wrong thing.

title: Stop Trying to Delight Your Customers (Matthew Dixon, Karen Freeman and Nick Toman, Harvard Business Review, July-August 2010)
supports: Opened with WebFetch (paywalled; opening only). Authors and issue date; questions the belief that companies must delight customers, noting that customers rarely choose a company because of over-the-top service. The effort argument beyond the opening is not visible on the page and is not cited from it.

title: Net Promoter Score: What a Customer-Relations Metric Can Tell You About Your User Experience (Therese Fessenden, 21 June 2024)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. NPS shows how an experience is perceived, not why; scale use differs by culture (net-negative scores in Japan and South Korea even for liked companies); it measures stated intent; binning discards information; small samples are unreliable; weak for detecting small design changes; can be gamed once it becomes a target; pair with behaviour measures and follow-up questions and report a margin of error.

title: Measuring user satisfaction (Service Manual, updated 19 February 2021)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Collect feedback at the end of the service and at every end point, provide in-service feedback, record where users drop out, measure assisted channels such as phone; include an open question on how to improve; look for statistically significant patterns; combine satisfaction with feedback, drop-out points and analytics; test changes and keep monitoring.

title: UK Customer Satisfaction Index (July 2026)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. July 2026 UKCSI 78.3 out of 100, up 1 point on a year earlier and 0.1 on January 2026; 59,500 responses from an online panel; banks and building societies highest sector at 82.0; five dimensions (experience, complaints handling, customer ethos, emotional connection, ethics); customers rate experiences from the previous three months.

title: UX Mapping Methods Compared: A Cheat Sheet (Sarah Gibbons, 5 November 2017)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Four mapping methods compared: empathy map (one user type, not sequential), what this kit calls a customer path map (one persona's steps, thoughts and emotions toward a goal with a product or service; the article uses the field's usual name), experience map (general behaviour, product-agnostic) and service blueprint (the provider's people, props and processes behind each touchpoint); combinations are usually most useful.

title: Service Blueprints: Definition (Sarah Gibbons, 27 August 2017, reviewed 15 July 2026)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Blueprint lanes: customer actions, frontstage, backstage, supporting processes and evidence; lines of interaction, visibility and internal interaction; optional time, policy, employee emotion and metrics; one blueprint per scenario; best for complex services with many touchpoints or several departments.

title: Service Design 101 (Sarah Gibbons, 9 July 2017)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Service design organises people, props and processes; frontstage elements customers see and backstage policies, systems and infrastructure they do not; backstage processes shape the customer experience; information given to one agent should be available to every agent.

title: Designing Services That Deliver (G. Lynn Shostack, Harvard Business Review, January 1984)
supports: Opened with WebFetch (paywalled; opening only). Author was a senior vice president at Bankers Trust; January 1984; opens with everyday service failures such as a laundry returning a shirt with a broken button and an ATM that swallows a card.

title: EAST: Four simple ways to apply behavioural insights (first published 2014, updated 16 December 2024)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Behaviour change is more likely when the desired behaviour is made Easy, Attractive, Social and Timely; published by BIT (part of Nesta) in 2014 and revised in December 2024.

title: MRS Code of Conduct 2023
supports: Opened with WebFetch; PDF text extracted locally. Rule 28 on fit-for-purpose, unbiased data collection; rule 29 requires telling participants about recording, monitoring or observation at recruitment and at the start, and its comment says mystery shopping can only be recorded in own-organisation mystery shopping where staff have been told; points to an MRS guideline on conducting mystery shopping.

title: How to complain (consumers)
supports: Opened with WebFetch (no page date). Complain to the business first; most complaints allow up to 8 weeks, fraud and scams, payment services and e-money 15 days; bring the complaint to the ombudsman within 6 months of the final response, or when the business runs out of time; the service is free.

title: How to settle complaints (for businesses)
supports: Opened with WebFetch (no page date). FCA-regulated businesses follow the DISP rules; prompt written acknowledgement, or a summary resolution if settled within 3 business days; a final response summarises the complaint, owns mistakes, gives the decision and reasons, says whether time limits are waived (DISP 1 Annex 3R wording), gives the ombudsman's details and the consumer leaflet, and the six-month referral right; keep the customer informed; consider the Consumer Duty.

title: Time limits for businesses
supports: Opened with WebFetch (no page date). 15 days for fraud and scams and for payment services and e-money; 8 weeks for most other complaints; if time runs out, send a final response or explain the delay, give referral rights and the leaflet; consumers usually have 6 years to complain, or 3 years from awareness, and 6 months after a final response; proactive settlement within 14 days of an investigation starting.

title: Consumer Duty
supports: Opened with WebFetch (no page date; latest publication listed 29 October 2026). The Duty sets high standards of protection for retail consumers across financial services and requires firms to put customers' needs first; links to the final rules and recent publications, including one on customers in vulnerable circumstances at payments firms (17 September 2026).

title: Learn how the complaint process works (last modified 5 October 2026)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. CFPB routes complaints to companies; companies generally respond within 15 days, and in some cases give a final response within 60 days; complaints are published in the public Consumer Complaint Database without directly identifying details; consumers have 60 days to give feedback; complaints are shared with other agencies.

title: Chatbots in consumer finance (6 June 2023, page modified 24 October 2024)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Customers expect timely, straightforward answers whatever the technology; firms are likely to shift support toward AI tools; deficient chatbots that prevent access to live, human support can lead to law violations and lower service quality.

title: Alternative dispute resolution for consumers
supports: Opened with WebFetch (no page date). ADR settles complaints out of court through impartial bodies (mediation, ombudsmen, arbitration, complaints boards); lists of bodies by country; the Commission proposed on 17 October 2023 to amend the ADR Directive and repeal the ODR Regulation, and a discontinuation document for the ODR platform is dated 19 December 2024.

title: AI Act, Article 50: Transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems
publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
supports: Opened with WebFetch (text based on the consolidated version as at 27 July 2026). Article 50(1): providers must design AI systems that interact directly with people so they are informed they are dealing with an AI, unless obvious to a reasonably well-informed person; 50(3) emotion recognition notice by deployers; 50(5) information at the latest at the first interaction, clear, distinguishable and accessible.

title: Transparency obligations under Article 50 of the AI Act (questions and answers, updated 24 July 2026)
publisher: European Commission, Shaping Europe's digital future
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Chatbots, AI agents and avatars are examples; four cumulative criteria for direct interaction; the obvious exception is read restrictively; notice from the start of the first interaction; provider and deployer defined; Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026, with a transition to 2 December 2026 only for the marking duty in 50(2).

title: AI Act, Article 113: Entry into force and application
publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
supports: Opened with WebFetch. The general application date is 2 August 2026; Chapter IV (Article 50) is not among the exceptions, and the amendment tags on the page do not affect it.

title: Complying with consumer law when using AI agents (updated 30 October 2026)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Businesses are responsible for what their AI agents do, even if a third party supplied them; agents must not mislead on prices, products or consumer rights; label AI agents where it could affect decisions and do not imply a real person; test before deployment and keep a human in the loop; breaches can lead to fines of up to 10% of worldwide turnover and compensation.

title: FTC Announces Crackdown on Deceptive AI Claims and Schemes (25 September 2024)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Operation AI Comply: the FTC chair said using AI tools to trick, mislead or defraud people is illegal and there is no AI exemption from existing law; five actions including DoNotPay ($193,000 proposed settlement) and Rytr (AI-generated fake reviews).

title: Klarna AI assistant handles two-thirds of customer service chats in its first month (27 February 2024)
supports: Opened with WebFetch. Company's own claims, with no method given: 2.3 million conversations in about a month, two-thirds of its service chats, work equal to about 700 full-time agents, satisfaction on a par with human agents, repeat inquiries down 25%, resolution time from 11 minutes to under 2, 23 markets and more than 35 languages.
